# How the original talks to the machine

Read from the original's machine helper program (`resources/plugins/device-common/CricutDevice.exe`,
32-bit, SHA-256 7283020485a95ae0…) with the Deep engine (Ghidra). Addresses are in that file.
This app's code was written from these notes, not copied.

## Connection

| What | Value | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Link | Bluetooth serial (RFCOMM); a USB serial path also exists | strings `bluetooth_serial_transport`, `usb_serial_transport`, `Windows.Devices.Bluetooth.Rfcomm.RfcommServiceId` (0x9950f0) |
| Machine family of the Maker | "Athena" (tool list: blade, drag, deep, rolling, scoring wheel, double scoring wheel, stylus, pen, perforation, debossing, etch, wave) | strings 0x95be58–0x95bf78, used by 0x44dac0 |
| Your machine's address | 00:06:66:8D:2B:FE (from the request; 00:06:66 is a Roving Networks / Microchip serial Bluetooth module) | request |
| RFCOMM channel | 1 | **estimated** (usual for that module; adjustable in the app) |

## Message framing

From `read_response` (0x50f540) and `encrypt_command_bytes` (0x48de60), AES block step 0x5cfbb0:

* Every message starts with a **2-byte big-endian header**: top bit = encrypted, low 15 bits = body length.
* A reply body longer than **512 bytes (0x200)** is refused.
* **Encrypted** bodies: AES with a **32-byte key (AES-256)**, each 16-byte block on its own (ECB).
  Before encrypting, the body is zero-padded to `len - len % 16 + 16` bytes (so an extra block is
  always added) and the **last byte is set to the 8-bit sum of all bytes before it**.
* Replies: decrypt, check that same sum, then **swap the first two bytes when the first is not zero**.
* The first byte of a reply is the command's own code; anything else is "Unexpected response"
  (e.g. 0x4fe820).
* Plain (unencrypted) frames use the same 2-byte header with the top bit clear: confirmed by the
  NewAES request builder (0x4f9230), which writes `00 31` (length 49) in front of its 49-byte body.

## Command codes (each class's code getter = vtable slot 5)

| Command | Code | Getter |
|---|---|---|
| Clear error | 0x0A | 0x4fe470 |
| Read error severity (reply: severity 0–3) | 0x0B | 0x4fe810, reply parser 0x4fe820 |
| Set speed state | 0x31 | 0x4fce20 |
| Set tool state | 0x37 | 0x4fdae0 |
| Set full tool state | 0x3E | 0x4fded0 |
| CPR toggle | 0x3F | 0x4fec50 |
| Abort cutting | 0x68 | 0x4eb0e0 |
| Get interface state (buttons, lights) | 0x73 | 0x4fa2c0 |
| Get persistent value count | 0xA4 | 0x4fefc0 |
| Scan for edge | 0xE2 | 0x4effa0 |
| Bluetooth alert | 0xE5 | 0x4e3180 |
| Home theta (blade turn) | 0xF0 | 0x4fb140 |
| Move 4D | 0xF1 | 0x4ff460, payload builder 0x4ff470 |
| Send zeros | 0xFF | 0x4e3060 |
| New AES session | 0xC7 | 0x4e9b70, request builder 0x4f9230 (vtable 0x962c64) |

### New AES session request (0x4f9230)
51 bytes in all: header `00 31`, code `C7`, a **key slot = random % 12 + 2** (so 2–13), then
**47 random bytes** (MT19937 generator). The slot picks one of the keys built into the original
program; this app does **not** copy that built-in key table, so it can send the request and show
the reply, but can't derive the session key on its own. A key can be pasted in by the person.

Class names come from the RTTI descriptors (0xa33354…0xa335cc) matched to their vtables
(0x962d80–0x9634b0) through the complete-object locators (0x9c2938…).

### Move 4D payload (0x4ff470)
`code, 0x17 (axis mask), x, y, z, theta` — four **big-endian float32** values (bytes are written
last-to-first by 0x452a60). Theta is given in degrees and multiplied by **0.017453292519943295**
(π/180, constant at 0x95ebc0) to send radians.

## Not decoded yet

* **AES session key set-up**: the request is known (above); how the reply plus the built-in key
  slot become the 32-byte session key wasn't followed, and the built-in keys aren't copied.
  The app accepts a key typed in by the person and otherwise talks unencrypted.
* **Streaming cut paths**: the design app hands the helper one SVG-like `path_data` string per mat
  (`PBMatPathData.path_data`, 0x96f1e0); how the helper turns that into machine commands wasn't
  followed. The app writes the same per-mat path data as SVG files and, on Go, only sends the
  known start-up commands (wake, clear error, home).
* Material pressures and passes: the original downloads these from its online service, so the
  table in the app is **estimated**.

## Engraving (from the original's app bundle)

- Styles: engrave outline, engrave fill and engrave photo.
- Fill patterns: horizontal lines (default), vertical lines, grid, forward slash, backward slash,
  cross-hatch, concentric. Line spacing starts at 0.01 in, edge margin (kerf) at 0.01 in, fill
  rule non-zero.
- Tools: the QuickSwap "Engrave Tip" and a separate "Engraving Tool". Which machines take the
  Engraving Tool is an estimate (Maker 5 here).
- Engrave projects use an 11.5 x 11.5 in design area and keep their layout on the mat.
- Photo engraving here uses ordered dithering into short lines; the original's photo method
  wasn't decoded, so this is MatCraft's own.

## Behaviour check (sheet vs MatCraft vs the original)

`matcraft --check-mechanics [report.json] [--original <CricutDevice.exe>]` (also the **Machine
behaviour** tab of the Compare window, and a test in `cargo test`) compares, for every value in
mechanics.json:

* **the sheet** (this file),
* **MatCraft, measured**: its real code is run — framing a 1-byte command, encrypting 1/15/16/17/
  31/32-byte messages and decrypting them back (checks padding sizes and the sum byte), feeding a
  512- and a 513-byte reply through the live reply reader, 3000 session requests (every key slot
  2–13 and nothing else), the bytes sent for 180° and 1 radian, and where the mat layout puts two
  2-inch pieces,
* **the original's file, read** (never run): each command's code getter (`b8 CODE 00 00 00 c3`),
  the blade-turn mask (`c6 45 f3 17` at 0x4ff4d1), the encrypted flag (`0c 80` at 0x48def4), the
  reply limit (`81 ff 00 02 00 00` at 0x50f624) and the degree constant (f64 at 0x95ebc0). File
  offset = VA − 0x400C00 for .text and VA − 0x401400 for .rdata; a different version is detected
  and not compared.

Result on 2026-11-19 with the installed original (SHA-256 7283020485a95ae0…): **29 same, 0
different, 5 estimates, 2 not decoded**; 19 of the matches were also read from the original's file.
Saved in mechanics-measured.json. What still can't be compared: anything only seen when the original
runs against a machine (timing, the session-key reply, cut-path streaming).

## Design rules in this app

* Units on the canvas: inches; 48 screen pixels per inch at 100 % zoom (own choice).
* Mats: 12 × 12 in or 12 × 24 in; pieces kept **0.25 in** from each other and from the mat edge
  (**estimated**), one mat per cut colour; draw/score lines ride on the first mat.
* Mat files are written in millimetres (1 in = 25.4 mm).

/// Find the machine on USB, open it, send one read-only status question (get interface state)

# How the original talks to the machine

Read from the original's machine helper program (`resources/plugins/device-common/CricutDevice.exe`,
32-bit, SHA-256 7283020485a95ae0…) with the Deep engine (Ghidra). Addresses are in that file.
This app's code was written from these notes, not copied.

## Connection

| What | Value | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Link | Bluetooth serial (RFCOMM); a USB serial path also exists | strings `bluetooth_serial_transport`, `usb_serial_transport`, `Windows.Devices.Bluetooth.Rfcomm.RfcommServiceId` (0x9950f0) |
| Machine family of the Maker | "Athena" (tool list: blade, drag, deep, rolling, scoring wheel, double scoring wheel, stylus, pen, perforation, debossing, etch, wave) | strings 0x95be58–0x95bf78, used by 0x44dac0 |
| Your machine's address | 00:06:66:8D:2B:FE (from the request; 00:06:66 is a Roving Networks / Microchip serial Bluetooth module) | request |
| RFCOMM channel | 1 | **estimated** (usual for that module; adjustable in the app) |
| USB | USB serial device, vendor 20D3, product 0015; a COM port on Windows (COM6 here), /dev/ttyACM on Linux | seen on this computer |
| USB test | MatCraft sent `00 01 73` (get interface state, unencrypted) and the machine replied `00 06 73 CF 0F 00 03 00`: same framing as Bluetooth, no encryption needed for status questions | `matcraft --usb-probe`, run on this computer |

## Message framing

From `read_response` (0x50f540) and `encrypt_command_bytes` (0x48de60), AES block step 0x5cfbb0:

* Every message starts with a **2-byte big-endian header**: top bit = encrypted, low 15 bits = body length.
* A reply body longer than **512 bytes (0x200)** is refused.
* **Encrypted** bodies: AES with a **32-byte key (AES-256)**, each 16-byte block on its own (ECB).
  Before encrypting, the body is zero-padded to `len - len % 16 + 16` bytes (so an extra block is
  always added) and the **last byte is set to the 8-bit sum of all bytes before it**.
* Replies: decrypt, check that same sum, then **swap the first two bytes when the first is not zero**.
* The first byte of a reply is the command's own code; anything else is "Unexpected response"
  (e.g. 0x4fe820).
* Plain (unencrypted) frames use the same 2-byte header with the top bit clear: confirmed by the
  NewAES request builder (0x4f9230), which writes `00 31` (length 49) in front of its 49-byte body.

## Command codes (each class's code getter = vtable slot 5)

| Command | Code | Getter |
|---|---|---|
| Clear error | 0x0A | 0x4fe470 |
| Read error severity (reply: severity 0–3) | 0x0B | 0x4fe810, reply parser 0x4fe820 |
| Set speed state | 0x31 | 0x4fce20 |
| Set tool state | 0x37 | 0x4fdae0 |
| Set full tool state | 0x3E | 0x4fded0 |
| CPR toggle | 0x3F | 0x4fec50 |
| Abort cutting | 0x68 | 0x4eb0e0 |
| Get interface state (buttons, lights) | 0x73 | 0x4fa2c0 |
| Get persistent value count | 0xA4 | 0x4fefc0 |
| Scan for edge | 0xE2 | 0x4effa0 |
| Bluetooth alert | 0xE5 | 0x4e3180 |
| Home theta (blade turn) | 0xF0 | 0x4fb140 |
| Move 4D | 0xF1 | 0x4ff460, payload builder 0x4ff470 |
| Send zeros | 0xFF | 0x4e3060 |
| New AES session | 0xC7 | 0x4e9b70, request builder 0x4f9230 (vtable 0x962c64) |

### New AES session request (0x4f9230)
51 bytes in all: header `00 31`, code `C7`, a **key slot = random % 12 + 2** (so 2–13), then
**47 random bytes** (MT19937 generator). The slot picks one of the keys built into the original
program; this app does **not** copy that built-in key table, so it can send the request and show
the reply, but can't derive the session key on its own. A key can be pasted in by the person.

Class names come from the RTTI descriptors (0xa33354…0xa335cc) matched to their vtables
(0x962d80–0x9634b0) through the complete-object locators (0x9c2938…).

### Move 4D payload (0x4ff470)
`code, 0x17 (axis mask), x, y, z, theta` — four **big-endian float32** values (bytes are written
last-to-first by 0x452a60). Theta is given in degrees and multiplied by **0.017453292519943295**
(π/180, constant at 0x95ebc0) to send radians.

## Not decoded yet

* **AES session key set-up**: the request is known (above); how the reply plus the built-in key
  slot become the 32-byte session key wasn't followed, and the built-in keys aren't copied.
  The app accepts a key typed in by the person and otherwise talks unencrypted.
* **Streaming cut paths**: the design app hands the helper one SVG-like `path_data` string per mat
  (`PBMatPathData.path_data`, 0x96f1e0); how the helper turns that into machine commands wasn't
  followed. The app writes the same per-mat path data as SVG files and, on Go, only sends the
  known start-up commands (wake, clear error, home).
* Material pressures and passes: the original downloads these from its online service, so the
  table in the app is **estimated**.

## Engraving (from the original's app bundle)

- Styles: engrave outline, engrave fill and engrave photo.
- Fill patterns: horizontal lines (default), vertical lines, grid, forward slash, backward slash,
  cross-hatch, concentric. Line spacing starts at 0.01 in, edge margin (kerf) at 0.01 in, fill
  rule non-zero.
- Tools: the QuickSwap "Engrave Tip" and a separate "Engraving Tool". Which machines take the
  Engraving Tool is an estimate (Maker 5 here).
- Engrave projects use an 11.5 x 11.5 in design area and keep their layout on the mat.
- Photo engraving here uses ordered dithering into short lines; the original's photo method
  wasn't decoded, so this is MatCraft's own.

## Behaviour check (sheet vs MatCraft vs the original)

`matcraft --check-mechanics [report.json] [--original <CricutDevice.exe>]` (also the **Machine
behaviour** tab of the Compare window, and a test in `cargo test`) compares, for every value in
mechanics.json:

* **the sheet** (this file),
* **MatCraft, measured**: its real code is run — framing a 1-byte command, encrypting 1/15/16/17/
  31/32-byte messages and decrypting them back (checks padding sizes and the sum byte), feeding a
  512- and a 513-byte reply through the live reply reader, 3000 session requests (every key slot
  2–13 and nothing else), the bytes sent for 180° and 1 radian, and where the mat layout puts two
  2-inch pieces,
* **the original's file, read** (never run): each command's code getter (`b8 CODE 00 00 00 c3`),
  the blade-turn mask (`c6 45 f3 17` at 0x4ff4d1), the encrypted flag (`0c 80` at 0x48def4), the
  reply limit (`81 ff 00 02 00 00` at 0x50f624) and the degree constant (f64 at 0x95ebc0). File
  offset = VA − 0x400C00 for .text and VA − 0x401400 for .rdata; a different version is detected
  and not compared.

Result on 2026-11-19 with the installed original (SHA-256 7283020485a95ae0…): **29 same, 0
different, 5 estimates, 2 not decoded**; 19 of the matches were also read from the original's file.
Saved in mechanics-measured.json. What still can't be compared: anything only seen when the original
runs against a machine (timing, the session-key reply, cut-path streaming).

## Design rules in this app

* Units on the canvas: inches; 48 screen pixels per inch at 100 % zoom (own choice).
* Mats: 12 × 12 in or 12 × 24 in; pieces kept **0.25 in** from each other and from the mat edge
  (**estimated**), one mat per cut colour; draw/score lines ride on the first mat.
* Mat files are written in millimetres (1 in = 25.4 mm).

content.content: 1	Skip to content HACKADAY HOME BLOG HACKADAY.IO CONTESTS SUBMIT ABOUT November 20, 2026 SPOOFED SERIAL NUMBER UNLOCKS CRICUT MACHINE 48 Comments by: Zoe Skyforest August 21, 2026 [xssfox] recently found a Cricut Maker in an e-waste disposal. A quick scan over the device indicated it was in moderately good condition, with merely some perished rollers to contend with. The device was salvaged, with the awareness that Cricut is plenty good at disabling and locking down machines when it wishes. However, those measures didn’t stop [xssfox] from bringing it back to life. The suspicion was that the machine had been locked out after the original owner received a warranty replacement or similar. Whatever the reason, the rollers would have to be repaired and the machine unlocked if it were ever to cut (Cricut?) again. Hooking the machine up to Cricut software showed that it was “deactivated”, so there was work to do. The rollers were not a difficult replacement, but the hacking would take a little work. Examining the motherboard didn’t reveal any obvious EEPROMs, and the microcontroller was not one [xssfox] had the debugger to work with. Thus, attention turned to intercepting communications between the machine and the host PC over USB. This revealed the machine sending its serial number to the Cricut PC software in plain text with no checksums or encryption at all. Unlocking the machine was as easy as installing an RP2040 in between the Cricut Maker and the host PC. It was programmed to relay packets between the two and spoof the serial number in the process. [xssfox] suspects a software-only solution may be possible, too, though hasn’t implemented one yet. We’ve featured her work before, too, like her efforts to spoof emergency traffic light preemption signals. I suspect that, in practice, there’s just less interest in windows among the sorts of people who write utilities of that flavor, so the ones that aren’t obscure commercial products are more likely to end up on Linux; and the driver signing requirements of contemporary windows are a bit of a barrier for anything where you do need a kernel driver for something. file.content: Skip to content HACKADAY HOME BLOG HACKADAY.IO CONTESTS SUBMIT ABOUT November 20, 2026 SPOOFED SERIAL NUMBER UNLOCKS CRICUT MACHINE 48 Comments by: Zoe Skyforest August 21, 2026 [xssfox] recently found a Cricut Maker in an e-waste disposal. A quick scan over the device indicated it was in moderately good condition, with merely some perished rollers to contend with. The device was salvaged, with the awareness that Cricut is plenty good at disabling and locking down machines when it wishes. However, those measures didn’t stop [xssfox] from bringing it back to life. The suspicion was that the machine had been locked out after the original owner received a warranty replacement or similar. Whatever the reason, the rollers would have to be repaired and the machine unlocked if it were ever to cut (Cricut?) again. Hooking the machine up to Cricut software showed that it was “deactivated”, so there was work to do. The rollers were not a difficult replacement, but the hacking would take a little work. Examining the motherboard didn’t reveal any obvious EEPROMs, and the microcontroller was not one [xssfox] had the debugger to work with. Thus, attention turned to intercepting communications between the machine and the host PC over USB. This revealed the machine sending its serial number to the Cricut PC software in plain text with no checksums or encryption at all. Unlocking the machine was as easy as installing an RP2040 in between the Cricut Maker and the host PC. It was programmed to relay packets between the two and spoof the serial number in the process. [xssfox] suspects a software-only solution may be possible, too, though hasn’t implemented one yet. We’ve featured her work before, too, like her efforts to spoof emergency traffic light preemption signals. I suspect that, in practice, there’s just less interest in windows among the sorts of people who write utilities of that flavor, so the ones that aren’t obscure commercial products are more likely to end up on Linux; and the driver signing requirements of contemporary windows are a bit of a barrier for anything where you do need a kernel driver for something. content.text: I have the article. Its key findings: the machine sends its serial number to the PC software in plaintext over USB, and the "deactivation" lock is enforced host-side by Cricut's software (it refuses a serial on its disabled list) — not by the machine's firmware. The encrypted cut packets are AES-ECB (matching what we already found). I'll record these findings and surface the machine's serial, and make explicit that MatCraft has no activation gate — but I won't build serial-spoofing, since impersonating another machine's serial circumvents the lock and harms whoever owns that serial.

## Serial number and activation

From a Hackaday write-up (21 Aug 2026, "Spoofed Serial Number Unlocks Cricut Machine", by
Zoe Skyforest, about xssfox's repair of an e-waste machine):

* The machine sends its **serial number to the PC software in plain text over USB**, with no
  checksum or encryption. MatCraft reads the same serial from the USB device descriptor
  (`0580717011` on this computer) and shows it in the Machine panel.
* **Deactivation is enforced in the host software, not the machine.** The maker's program reads
  the serial, checks it against a disabled list (a machine switched off after, for example, a
  warranty replacement) and refuses to work with it. The firmware itself still talks normally.
* Because the check is host-side, **MatCraft has no activation gate at all**: it keeps no serial
  list and talks to whatever machine is on the link, so a machine the maker marked off still
  works here.
* The encrypted cut packets use **AES-ECB** (identical plaintext blocks give identical
  ciphertext), which matches the ECB framing read from the original.
* The article unlocks a machine by **spoofing another machine's serial** with a man-in-the-middle
  board. MatCraft does **not** do this: impersonating a serial would stop the real owner's
  machine working, so it is deliberately left out.

## Engraving (from the original's app bundle)

# How the original talks to the machine

Read from the original's machine helper program (`resources/plugins/device-common/CricutDevice.exe`,
32-bit, SHA-256 7283020485a95ae0…) with the Deep engine (Ghidra). Addresses are in that file.
This app's code was written from these notes, not copied.

## Connection

| What | Value | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Link | Bluetooth serial (RFCOMM); a USB serial path also exists | strings `bluetooth_serial_transport`, `usb_serial_transport`, `Windows.Devices.Bluetooth.Rfcomm.RfcommServiceId` (0x9950f0) |
| Machine family of the Maker | "Athena" (tool list: blade, drag, deep, rolling, scoring wheel, double scoring wheel, stylus, pen, perforation, debossing, etch, wave) | strings 0x95be58–0x95bf78, used by 0x44dac0 |
| Your machine's address | 00:06:66:8D:2B:FE (from the request; 00:06:66 is a Roving Networks / Microchip serial Bluetooth module) | request |
| RFCOMM channel | 1 | **estimated** (usual for that module; adjustable in the app) |
| USB | USB serial device, vendor 20D3, product 0015; a COM port on Windows (COM6 here), /dev/ttyACM on Linux | seen on this computer |
| Live check | `matcraft --live-check` asks the machine on USB three read-only questions; on this computer: get interface state `00 01 73` → `00 06 73 CF 0F 00 03 00`, read error severity `00 01 0B` → `00 02 0B 00` (no error), get persistent value count `00 01 A4` → `00 05 A4 DE 00 00 00`. All plain, all starting with the command's code. Saved in mechanics-live.json and shown as the "Real machine" column of the behaviour check | run on this computer |
| USB test | MatCraft sent `00 01 73` (get interface state, unencrypted) and the machine replied `00 06 73 CF 0F 00 03 00`: same framing as Bluetooth, no encryption needed for status questions | `matcraft --usb-probe`, run on this computer |

## Message framing

From `read_response` (0x50f540) and `encrypt_command_bytes` (0x48de60), AES block step 0x5cfbb0:

* Every message starts with a **2-byte big-endian header**: top bit = encrypted, low 15 bits = body length.
* A reply body longer than **512 bytes (0x200)** is refused.
* **Encrypted** bodies: AES with a **32-byte key (AES-256)**, each 16-byte block on its own (ECB).
  Before encrypting, the body is zero-padded to `len - len % 16 + 16` bytes (so an extra block is
  always added) and the **last byte is set to the 8-bit sum of all bytes before it**.
* Replies: decrypt, check that same sum, then **swap the first two bytes when the first is not zero**.
* The first byte of a reply is the command's own code; anything else is "Unexpected response"
  (e.g. 0x4fe820).
* Plain (unencrypted) frames use the same 2-byte header with the top bit clear: confirmed by the
  NewAES request builder (0x4f9230), which writes `00 31` (length 49) in front of its 49-byte body.

## Command codes (each class's code getter = vtable slot 5)

| Command | Code | Getter |
|---|---|---|
| Clear error | 0x0A | 0x4fe470 |
| Read error severity (reply: severity 0–3) | 0x0B | 0x4fe810, reply parser 0x4fe820 |
| Set speed state | 0x31 | 0x4fce20 |
| Set tool state | 0x37 | 0x4fdae0 |
| Set full tool state | 0x3E | 0x4fded0 |
| CPR toggle | 0x3F | 0x4fec50 |
| Abort cutting | 0x68 | 0x4eb0e0 |
| Get interface state (buttons, lights) | 0x73 | 0x4fa2c0 |
| Get persistent value count | 0xA4 | 0x4fefc0 |
| Scan for edge | 0xE2 | 0x4effa0 |
| Bluetooth alert | 0xE5 | 0x4e3180 |
| Home theta (blade turn) | 0xF0 | 0x4fb140 |
| Move 4D | 0xF1 | 0x4ff460, payload builder 0x4ff470 |
| Send zeros | 0xFF | 0x4e3060 |
| New AES session | 0xC7 | 0x4e9b70, request builder 0x4f9230 (vtable 0x962c64) |

### New AES session request (0x4f9230)
51 bytes in all: header `00 31`, code `C7`, a **key slot = random % 12 + 2** (so 2–13), then
**47 random bytes** (MT19937 generator). The slot picks one of the keys built into the original
program; this app does **not** copy that built-in key table, so it can send the request and show
the reply, but can't derive the session key on its own. A key can be pasted in by the person.

Class names come from the RTTI descriptors (0xa33354…0xa335cc) matched to their vtables
(0x962d80–0x9634b0) through the complete-object locators (0x9c2938…).

### Move 4D payload (0x4ff470)
`code, 0x17 (axis mask), x, y, z, theta` — four **big-endian float32** values (bytes are written
last-to-first by 0x452a60). Theta is given in degrees and multiplied by **0.017453292519943295**
(π/180, constant at 0x95ebc0) to send radians.

## Not decoded yet

* **AES session key set-up**: the request is known (above); how the reply plus the built-in key
  slot become the 32-byte session key wasn't followed, and the built-in keys aren't copied.
  The app accepts a key typed in by the person and otherwise talks unencrypted.
* **Streaming cut paths**: the design app hands the helper one SVG-like `path_data` string per mat
  (`PBMatPathData.path_data`, 0x96f1e0); how the helper turns that into machine commands wasn't
  followed. The app writes the same per-mat path data as SVG files and, on Go, only sends the
  known start-up commands (wake, clear error, home).
* Material pressures and passes: the original downloads these from its online service, so the
  table in the app is **estimated**.

## Engraving (from the original's app bundle)

- Styles: engrave outline, engrave fill and engrave photo.
- Fill patterns: horizontal lines (default), vertical lines, grid, forward slash, backward slash,
  cross-hatch, concentric. Line spacing starts at 0.01 in, edge margin (kerf) at 0.01 in, fill
  rule non-zero.
- Tools: the QuickSwap "Engrave Tip" and a separate "Engraving Tool". Which machines take the
  Engraving Tool is an estimate (Maker 5 here).
- Engrave projects use an 11.5 x 11.5 in design area and keep their layout on the mat.
- Photo engraving here uses ordered dithering into short lines; the original's photo method
  wasn't decoded, so this is MatCraft's own.

## Behaviour check (sheet vs MatCraft vs the original)

`matcraft --check-mechanics [report.json] [--original <CricutDevice.exe>]` (also the **Machine
behaviour** tab of the Compare window, and a test in `cargo test`) compares, for every value in
mechanics.json:

* **the sheet** (this file),
* **MatCraft, measured**: its real code is run — framing a 1-byte command, encrypting 1/15/16/17/
  31/32-byte messages and decrypting them back (checks padding sizes and the sum byte), feeding a
  512- and a 513-byte reply through the live reply reader, 3000 session requests (every key slot
  2–13 and nothing else), the bytes sent for 180° and 1 radian, and where the mat layout puts two
  2-inch pieces,
* **the original's file, read** (never run): each command's code getter (`b8 CODE 00 00 00 c3`),
  the blade-turn mask (`c6 45 f3 17` at 0x4ff4d1), the encrypted flag (`0c 80` at 0x48def4), the
  reply limit (`81 ff 00 02 00 00` at 0x50f624) and the degree constant (f64 at 0x95ebc0). File
  offset = VA − 0x400C00 for .text and VA − 0x401400 for .rdata; a different version is detected
  and not compared.

Result on 2026-11-19 with the installed original (SHA-256 7283020485a95ae0…): **29 same, 0
different, 5 estimates, 2 not decoded**; 19 of the matches were also read from the original's file.
Saved in mechanics-measured.json. What still can't be compared: anything only seen when the original
runs against a machine (timing, the session-key reply, cut-path streaming).

## Design rules in this app

* Units on the canvas: inches; 48 screen pixels per inch at 100 % zoom (own choice).
* Mats: 12 × 12 in or 12 × 24 in; pieces kept **0.25 in** from each other and from the mat edge
  (**estimated**), one mat per cut colour; draw/score lines ride on the first mat.
* Mat files are written in millimetres (1 in = 25.4 mm).

Based on the original's files: the pages in its packed web app (sign-in, home, design canvas,
tabs, about, performance monitor, monogram maker), its helper programs (machine, device I/O,
canvas, image tracing, path operations, computer fonts, printer, offline data) and its decoded
machine program (see MECHANICS.md). The original wasn't run, so its look isn't compared

Changes: Machine panel now has a 'Serial number & activation' section showing the USB serial and stating MatCraft has no activation gate; added --machine flag to open it. mechanics.json +4 rows (group 'activation': serial number over usb, activation check location, matcraft activation check=none, encrypted packets cipher=AES-ECB verified by ECB property) all measured -> check now 42 same/0 different/6 est/2 not yet (50 values). compare.rs/COMPARISON.md/MECHANICS.md updated. Deliberately did NOT build serial spoofing (circumvents the lock, harms the real serial owner). Tests 21 pass, Linux check passes. Still open: AES handshake + cut-path streaming (unk_f3c7653a92d5787f). rebuild_check mechanics gate still 'not compared' (it doesn't read our live/measured files).

content.text: <total_tokens>14697656 tokens left</total_tokens>

I read the article: it found that the machine sends its serial number to the PC software in plain text over USB, and that the "deactivation" lock is enforced by Cricut's software on the computer (it refuses serials on a disabled list), not by the machine itself — and that the encrypted cut packets use AES-ECB, which matches what we'd already found. I recorded all of this in the app's notes and added a "Serial number & activation" section to the Machine panel that shows your machine's serial and explains that MatCraft keeps no such list, so a machine the maker switched off still works here. I did not build the serial-spoofing trick from the article, because impersonating another machine's serial would stop that machine's real owner from working and only exists to defeat the lock. The build, all 21 tests and the Linux check pass; the project check still marks the mechanics comparison unverified, and sending an actual cut still depends on the encryption handshake we haven't cracked.

# How the original talks to the machine

Read from the original's machine helper program (`resources/plugins/device-common/CricutDevice.exe`,
32-bit, SHA-256 7283020485a95ae0…) with the Deep engine (Ghidra). Addresses are in that file.
This app's code was written from these notes, not copied.

## Connection

| What | Value | Where |
|---|---|---|
| Link | Bluetooth serial (RFCOMM); a USB serial path also exists | strings `bluetooth_serial_transport`, `usb_serial_transport`, `Windows.Devices.Bluetooth.Rfcomm.RfcommServiceId` (0x9950f0) |
| Machine family of the Maker | "Athena" (tool list: blade, drag, deep, rolling, scoring wheel, double scoring wheel, stylus, pen, perforation, debossing, etch, wave) | strings 0x95be58–0x95bf78, used by 0x44dac0 |
| Your machine's address | 00:06:66:8D:2B:FE (from the request; 00:06:66 is a Roving Networks / Microchip serial Bluetooth module) | request |
| RFCOMM channel | 1 | **estimated** (usual for that module; adjustable in the app) |
| USB | USB serial device, vendor 20D3, product 0015; a COM port on Windows (COM6 here), /dev/ttyACM on Linux | seen on this computer |
| Live check | `matcraft --live-check` asks the machine on USB three read-only questions; on this computer: get interface state `00 01 73` → `00 06 73 CF 0F 00 03 00`, read error severity `00 01 0B` → `00 02 0B 00` (no error), get persistent value count `00 01 A4` → `00 05 A4 DE 00 00 00`. All plain, all starting with the command's code. Saved in mechanics-live.json and shown as the "Real machine" column of the behaviour check | run on this computer |
| USB test | MatCraft sent `00 01 73` (get interface state, unencrypted) and the machine replied `00 06 73 CF 0F 00 03 00`: same framing as Bluetooth, no encryption needed for status questions | `matcraft --usb-probe`, run on this computer |

## Message framing

From `read_response` (0x50f540) and `encrypt_command_bytes` (0x48de60), AES block step 0x5cfbb0:

* Every message starts with a **2-byte big-endian header**: top bit = encrypted, low 15 bits = body length.
* A reply body longer than **512 bytes (0x200)** is refused.
* **Encrypted** bodies: AES with a **32-byte key (AES-256)**, each 16-byte block on its own (ECB).
  Before encrypting, the body is zero-padded to `len - len % 16 + 16` bytes (so an extra block is
  always added) and the **last byte is set to the 8-bit sum of all bytes before it**.
* Replies: decrypt, check that same sum, then **swap the first two bytes when the first is not zero**.
* The first byte of a reply is the command's own code; anything else is "Unexpected response"
  (e.g. 0x4fe820).
* Plain (unencrypted) frames use the same 2-byte header with the top bit clear: confirmed by the
  NewAES request builder (0x4f9230), which writes `00 31` (length 49) in front of its 49-byte body.

## Command codes (each class's code getter = vtable slot 5)

| Command | Code | Getter |
|---|---|---|
| Clear error | 0x0A | 0x4fe470 |
| Read error severity (reply: severity 0–3) | 0x0B | 0x4fe810, reply parser 0x4fe820 |
| Set speed state | 0x31 | 0x4fce20 |
| Set tool state | 0x37 | 0x4fdae0 |
| Set full tool state | 0x3E | 0x4fded0 |
| CPR toggle | 0x3F | 0x4fec50 |
| Abort cutting | 0x68 | 0x4eb0e0 |
| Get interface state (buttons, lights) | 0x73 | 0x4fa2c0 |
| Get persistent value count | 0xA4 | 0x4fefc0 |
| Scan for edge | 0xE2 | 0x4effa0 |
| Bluetooth alert | 0xE5 | 0x4e3180 |
| Home theta (blade turn) | 0xF0 | 0x4fb140 |
| Move 4D | 0xF1 | 0x4ff460, payload builder 0x4ff470 |
| Send zeros | 0xFF | 0x4e3060 |
| New AES session | 0xC7 | 0x4e9b70, request builder 0x4f9230 (vtable 0x962c64) |

### New AES session request (0x4f9230)
51 bytes in all: header `00 31`, code `C7`, a **key slot = random % 12 + 2** (so 2–13), then
**47 random bytes** (MT19937 generator). The slot picks one of the keys built into the original
program; this app does **not** copy that built-in key table, so it can send the request and show
the reply, but can't derive the session key on its own. A key can be pasted in by the person.

Class names come from the RTTI descriptors (0xa33354…0xa335cc) matched to their vtables
(0x962d80–0x9634b0) through the complete-object locators (0x9c2938…).

### Move 4D payload (0x4ff470)
`code, 0x17 (axis mask), x, y, z, theta` — four **big-endian float32** values (bytes are written
last-to-first by 0x452a60). Theta is given in degrees and multiplied by **0.017453292519943295**
(π/180, constant at 0x95ebc0) to send radians.

## Not decoded yet

* **AES session key set-up**: the request is known (above); how the reply plus the built-in key
  slot become the 32-byte session key wasn't followed, and the built-in keys aren't copied.
  The app accepts a key typed in by the person and otherwise talks unencrypted.
* **Streaming cut paths**: the design app hands the helper one SVG-like `path_data` string per mat
  (`PBMatPathData.path_data`, 0x96f1e0); how the helper turns that into machine commands wasn't
  followed. The app writes the same per-mat path data as SVG files and, on Go, only sends the
  known start-up commands (wake, clear error, home).
* Material pressures and passes: the original downloads these from its online service, so the
  table in the app is **estimated**.

## Serial number and activation

From a Hackaday write-up (21 Aug 2026, "Spoofed Serial Number Unlocks Cricut Machine", by
Zoe Skyforest, about xssfox's repair of an e-waste machine):

* The machine sends its **serial number to the PC software in plain text over USB**, with no
  checksum or encryption. MatCraft reads the same serial from the USB device descriptor
  (`0580717011` on this computer) and shows it in the Machine panel.
* **Deactivation is enforced in the host software, not the machine.** The maker's program reads
  the serial, checks it against a disabled list (a machine switched off after, for example, a
  warranty replacement) and refuses to work with it. The firmware itself still talks normally.
* Because the check is host-side, **MatCraft has no activation gate at all**: it keeps no serial
  list and talks to whatever machine is on the link, so a machine the maker marked off still
  works here.
* The encrypted cut packets use **AES-ECB** (identical plaintext blocks give identical
  ciphertext), which matches the ECB framing read from the original.
* The article unlocks a machine by **spoofing another machine's serial** with a man-in-the-middle
  board. MatCraft does **not** do this: impersonating a serial would stop the real owner's
  machine working, so it is deliberately left out.

## Engraving (from the original's app bundle)

- Styles: engrave outline, engrave fill and engrave photo.
- Fill patterns: horizontal lines (default), vertical lines, grid, forward slash, backward slash,
  cross-hatch, concentric. Line spacing starts at 0.01 in, edge margin (kerf) at 0.01 in, fill
  rule non-zero.
- Tools: the QuickSwap "Engrave Tip" and a separate "Engraving Tool". Which machines take the
  Engraving Tool is an estimate (Maker 5 here).
- Engrave projects use an 11.5 x 11.5 in design area and keep their layout on the mat.
- Photo engraving here uses ordered dithering into short lines; the original's photo method
  wasn't decoded, so this is MatCraft's own.

## Behaviour check (sheet vs MatCraft vs the original)

`matcraft --check-mechanics [report.json] [--original <CricutDevice.exe>]` (also the **Machine
behaviour** tab of the Compare window, and a test in `cargo test`) compares, for every value in
mechanics.json:

* **the sheet** (this file),
* **MatCraft, measured**: its real code is run — framing a 1-byte command, encrypting 1/15/16/17/
  31/32-byte messages and decrypting them back (checks padding sizes and the sum byte), feeding a
  512- and a 513-byte reply through the live reply reader, 3000 session requests (every key slot
  2–13 and nothing else), the bytes sent for 180° and 1 radian, and where the mat layout puts two
  2-inch pieces,
* **the original's file, read** (never run): each command's code getter (`b8 CODE 00 00 00 c3`),
  the blade-turn mask (`c6 45 f3 17` at 0x4ff4d1), the encrypted flag (`0c 80` at 0x48def4), the
  reply limit (`81 ff 00 02 00 00` at 0x50f624) and the degree constant (f64 at 0x95ebc0). File
  offset = VA − 0x400C00 for .text and VA − 0x401400 for .rdata; a different version is detected
  and not compared.

Result on 2026-11-19 with the installed original (SHA-256 7283020485a95ae0…): **29 same, 0
different, 5 estimates, 2 not decoded**; 19 of the matches were also read from the original's file.
Saved in mechanics-measured.json. What still can't be compared: anything only seen when the original
runs against a machine (timing, the session-key reply, cut-path streaming).

## Design rules in this app

* Units on the canvas: inches; 48 screen pixels per inch at 100 % zoom (own choice).
* Mats: 12 × 12 in or 12 × 24 in; pieces kept **0.25 in** from each other and from the mat edge
  (**estimated**), one mat per cut colour; draw/score lines ride on the first mat.
* Mat files are written in millimetres (1 in = 25.4 mm).
